newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia students eye Australia despite racism row.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia students eye Australia despite racism row.

text.p: A higher number of Malaysians have applied for student visas for Australia in the past 5-1/2 months compared with the same period last year, figures from the Australian High Commission here show.
A spokeswoman for the commission gave the figures when asked whether the recent racism debate in Australia had affected the number of Malaysian students applying to go there.
Between July 1 and December 16, 1996, 1,471 student visas were issued to Malaysians compared with 1,271 in the same period last year, she said.
Malaysian students in Australia have been in the spotlight this week after a report that several have had "nasty experiences" involving racial abuse.
Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said on Monday the country might consider bringing back its students in Australia if reported threats against them were found to be serious.
"We want to get information on whether (the situation) is really dangerous. (If so) we will take action, whether by bringing them home or offering them protection," he told reporters.

The Australian High Commissioner to Malaysia, Bill Farmer, on Wednesday sent a letter to Malaysian newspapers expressing concerns about reported racial abuse faced by Malaysian student leader Adrina Shazlin Shukor.

Adrina, who is deputy president of the United Malays National Organisation (UMNO) political club in Melbourne, was verbally abused by an Australian youth for being Asian, the national Bernama news agency reported at the weekend. UNMO is the ruling party in Malaysia.
"The Australian government finds this sort of behaviour quite abhorrent and is committed to fighting racism wherever it occurs," Farmer said in his letter.
"This unfortunate incident involving Ms Adrina contrasts with the extremely positive welcome experienced by the vast majority of overseas students in Australia," he said.
With more than 11,000 Malaysian students in Australia, Farmer added that he "can fully understand" Malaysian leaders' need to respond to concerns about the welfare of students in Australia.
Racism has become a major issue in Australia since independent politician Pauline Hanson said in her maiden Parliament speech in September that the country was being swamped by Asians.
Hanson called for an immediate moratorium on immigration, but Australian leaders have distanced themselves from Hanson's comments and said she does not reflect the official view.
Farmer, in his letter, repeated that sentiment.
"...Please allow me to reiterate that the Australian government completely disassociates itself from any racist attitudes or actions," he wrote.
Asians make up about five percent of Australia's 18 million population.
